h1: How a digital marketing agency works behind the scenes
metaTitle: How Does a Digital Marketing Agency Work?
metaDescription: How does digital marketing agency work? Follow the money: a ₹1,00,000 retainer split into specialist hours, account management, tools and margin.
answer: A digital marketing agency sells a monthly retainer, then splits it between specialist delivery time, account management, tools, overhead and margin. On a ₹1,00,000 fee, roughly ₹45,000–₹55,000 buys actual specialist hours — about 40 to 60 hours a month across every discipline on your account. Ad spend is billed separately.
takeaways: Your fee buys **hours**, not outcomes. Work out how many hours it buys and most agency arguments resolve themselves.
At ₹1,00,000/month you're funding roughly two to three hours of specialist attention per working day, split across three or four disciplines.
One account manager typically carries 5–12 accounts. Ask the number before you sign — it predicts your response times better than any SLA.
Revision rounds are the most expensive thing in the agency model, and you control almost all of them.

sections.h2: The retainer is the unit everything runs on
body: Almost every digital marketing agency in India runs on the same machine: a fixed monthly fee, invoiced in advance, against a scope of deliverables. Ad spend sits outside that fee. GST sits on top of it.

The fee is not a price for a result. It's a price for capacity — a slice of a team's month. Everything an agency does internally is an attempt to fit your scope inside that slice profitably, and every frustration clients report traces back to that one constraint. Slow turnarounds, junior staff on the account, the strategist who vanishes after month two: all of it is the same arithmetic showing through.
So the useful question isn't "is this agency good". It's "how many hours of what seniority does this fee actually buy, and is that enough for what I'm asking".

callout.title: The scope-of-work document matters more than the deck
callout.body: The pitch deck describes ambition. The SOW describes what will actually be produced each month. If a deliverable isn't in the SOW with a number next to it, assume it won't happen.

body: Here's the arithmetic, using round numbers you can adjust for your own quote. These are structural shares typical of a small-to-mid Indian agency — not audited figures from anyone's books, and they move with city, seniority and how much sales costs the agency.

Take the delivery line seriously. A mid-level specialist in India costs an agency roughly ₹700–₹1,200 an hour once you load salary with PF, workspace, equipment and non-billable time. So ₹48,000 of delivery budget buys somewhere between 40 and 65 hours a month, spread across your SEO, paid, content and design work. That's two to three hours a working day, total, for your entire account.

callout.title: Why a ₹15,000 retainer can't work
callout.body: Run the same maths downward. After tools and overhead, ₹15,000 leaves around six to eight specialist hours a month — under two hours a week for your entire marketing. That isn't a cheap agency, it's a subscription to a monthly report.

sections.h2: Account managers, specialists, and the person you actually meet
body: Agencies are built in two layers. The account layer talks to you. The delivery layer does the work. They are rarely the same people, and the gap between them is the single most common complaint founders bring us about a previous agency.

This structure isn't dishonest — a specialist who spends their day on client calls stops being a specialist. It becomes a problem only when nobody tells you it exists, or when the strategist who won the pitch is never seen again.
bullets: **Account manager / client lead** — owns the relationship, the reporting and your approvals. Usually carries several accounts.
**Strategist or head of channel** — sets direction, reviews at milestones, often the person in the pitch. Sees your account a few hours a month.
**Channel specialists** — the SEO, paid media, content and design people who produce the work. You may never speak to them.
**Production and QA** — writers, designers, developers, often part-shared with other accounts or partly freelance.

callout.title: The question that saves a year
callout.body: "Which of the people in this meeting will touch my account weekly, and for how many hours?" Any agency that has planned the work answers in ten seconds. The rest hedge.

sections.h2: How many clients one account manager carries
body: This number quietly determines your experience, and almost nobody asks it. The ranges below reflect how the model is structured rather than any agency's published policy.

A boutique setup runs 3–6 accounts per manager and can hold real context on each. Mid-size agencies typically run 6–12. Volume shops selling ₹10,000–₹25,000 packages have to run 15–25 or the maths fails, which is why those accounts feel templated — they are, by necessity.

We took the same constraint to its logical end and cap intake at three new clients a month. That isn't a marketing line; it's what carrying a guarantee forces you to do. [Why we only take three clients a month](/journal/why-we-only-take-three-clients-a-month) explains the trade.

sections.h2: The approval loop is where your hours die
body: Inside the agency, the expensive part of a deliverable is rarely the first draft. It's rounds two, three and four — and the calendar days lost waiting for feedback that arrives in fragments.

A standard cycle runs brief, draft, internal QA, client review, revision, publish. Most contracts include two revision rounds. Every round beyond that comes out of somebody's delivery hours, which means it comes out of next week's work.
numbered: **Give feedback once, consolidated.** Three people sending separate comments over four days costs more hours than the draft did.
**Approve or reject, don't ponder.** Work sitting in your inbox still occupies the agency's plan for the month.
**Fix the brief, not the draft.** If two consecutive deliverables come back wrong, the brief is wrong. Rewriting drafts forever is the expensive way to discover that.
**Name one approver.** Committee review is the most reliable way to burn a retainer without producing anything.
**Watch scope creep in your own requests.** "Quick extra deck" is four hours that were allocated to something you'll miss later.

sections.h2: Media spend is not the fee — and the markup question
body: If the agency runs paid media, there are two numbers: the management fee and the ad spend. Keep them separate in your head and in the contract, because the way they're combined is where the industry gets sharp.

Three common models. A percentage of spend, usually 10–20% — simple, and it quietly rewards the agency for spending more of your money. A flat management fee, which is cleaner because the incentive doesn't track budget. Or a bundled figure where spend and fee arrive as one number, which is the one to check hardest.

The specific thing to ask: does the agency add a markup to media, and does it receive rebates or incentives from any platform or reseller. Both are legal. Both mean the number in your ad account is not the number leaving your bank.

Our own answer is on the [pricing page](/pricing): ad spend is billed separately at cost with zero media markup, and performance management runs ₹40,000 / ₹75,000 / ₹1,50,000 a month depending on channel count and scale. Same logic applies on the organic side — [where your retainer money actually goes](/journal/where-your-seo-retainer-money-actually-goes) breaks down the SEO version.

callout.title: Two things to own before you sign anything
callout.body: Your ad accounts and your analytics property, in your company's name, with the agency added as a user. Agencies that hold these on your behalf make leaving expensive — and you'll lose the historical data that makes the next agency effective.

faqs.q: What does a digital marketing agency actually do each month?
faqs.a: Plan, produce, publish, measure, report. In practice that means a monthly plan, a set of deliverables in the scope document, ongoing channel management, and a report. The volume of each is set by your fee, since the fee buys a fixed number of specialist hours.

faqs.q: Is a monthly retainer better than paying per project?
faqs.a: For anything continuous — SEO, paid media, social — a retainer fits, because the work never finishes. For a defined build like a website or a campaign launch, a project fee is cleaner. Paying a retainer for work that has an end date is how budgets quietly leak.

faqs.q: Why do agencies insist on a minimum contract term?
faqs.a: Onboarding costs them real hours they can't bill, so a three-month minimum lets them recover it. Twelve-month lock-ins with long notice periods are a different thing: those protect agency revenue, not your results. We work month-to-month after the first quarter with 30 days' notice.

faqs.q: Does the agency's fee include ad spend?
faqs.a: It shouldn't. Management fee and media budget are separate lines and should be invoiced separately. If a proposal quotes one combined number, ask exactly how much reaches the ad platform and whether any markup or platform rebate applies.

faqs.q: How do I know if my retainer is being spent on my account?
faqs.a: Ask for the monthly plan against the scope document, and check that named deliverables shipped. You won't get timesheets from most agencies, and honestly they'd be easy to fake. Delivered work against a written scope is the check that holds up.

faqs.q: How much should a digital marketing agency cost in India?
faqs.a: Serious multi-channel work generally starts around ₹75,000–₹1,00,000 a month, because that's where the arithmetic supports a real team. Below ₹40,000 you're buying one channel, part-time. Our own SEO starts at ₹75,000/mo, with smaller sites from ₹40,000.
